result.question: Why can a higher-power processor still be more energy-efficient for a particular task?
result.answer: A processor that consumes more power can still be more energy-efficient if it completes the task significantly faster.

retrieved_chunks.text: ENERGY AND ENERGY EFFICIENCY A processor that consumes more power can still be more energy-efficient if it completes the task significantly faster.

ENERGY AND ENERGY EFFICIENCY The key idea is that power and energy are not the same thing, and when comparing processors for a particular task, energy is usually the better metric. Question :Which Processor is Energy Efficient? Processor A Processor B Average power 120 W 100 W Execution time 7 s 10 s
ENERGY EFFICIENCY STRATEGIES • Race-to-halt • Processor is only part of system cost • Use faster, less energy-efficient processor to allow the rest of the system to halt

ENERGY EFFICIENCY STRATEGIES • 2. Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) is the adjustment of power and speed settings on a computing device's various processors, controller chips and peripheral devices to optimize resource allotment for tasks and maximize power saving when those resources are not needed. • If the current task is computationally intensive, meaning it requires the processor to consume more energy and run at a higher frequency, DVFS will ensure that the voltage and frequency increase to match the requirements. However,if the processor needs to run a low-priority or less computationally intensive task where high speed and throughput are not required,it will adjust accordingly.

MAXIMUM POWER A PROCESSOR EVER REQUIRES? A processor does not consume a constant amount of power. For example: When the CPU is idle → low power When running normal programs → moderate power When performing heavy calculations → high power During short bursts of activity → it may demand very high peak power
